prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Walking home I feel a presence following and realize he is always there that Native man with coal-black-hair who is my grandfather. In my first memories he is present, mostly wordless, resident in the house where I was born. My mother shows him the cleft in my chin identical to his. I am swaddled and blinking in the kitchen light. So we are introduced. We never part. Sometimes I forget he lodges in my house still the bone-house where my heart beats. I carry his mother’s framework a sturdy structure. I learn his birthright. I hear his mother’s teachings through what my mother said of her: She kept a pot of stew on the stove all day for anyone to eat. She never went to church but said you could be a good person anyway. She fed hoboes during the ‘30s, her back porch a regular stop-over. Every person has rights no matter what color. Be respectful. This son of hers, my grandfather, still walks the streets with me. Some twist of blood and heat still spark across the time bridge. Here, listen: Air draws through these lungs made from his. His blood still pulses through this hand.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Walking, Native, Sometimes

outputs.L1:
Walking home, I sense a presence trailing behind me, and I realize he has always been there—that Native man with coal-black hair who is my grandfather. He inhabits my earliest memories, mostly wordless, a quiet resident in the house where I was born. My mother shows him the cleft in my chin, identical to his own. I lie swaddled, blinking in the kitchen light. And so we are introduced. We have never since parted.

Sometimes I forget he still dwells within me—within this house of bone where my heart beats. I carry forward his mother's framework, a sturdy foundation. I learn of his birthright. I hear his mother's teachings through what my own mother told me of her: She kept a pot of stew simmering on the stove all day, for anyone who might need it. She never set foot in church, yet believed you could still be a good person. During the thirties, she fed hoboes who passed through, her back porch a familiar stop along their way. Every person has rights, she said, no matter their color. Be respectful.

This son of hers—my grandfather—still walks these streets beside me. Some current of blood and warmth continues to spark across the bridge of time. Listen: the air I breathe passes through lungs shaped from his. His blood still moves through this hand.
outputs.L2: On my way home, something trails behind me, and I recognize that he's never truly absent—this dark-haired Indigenous man who is my grandfather. He appears in my earliest recollections, saying little, simply existing within the walls of the house where I entered the world. There, my mother pointed out to him the matching indentation in my chin, a mirror of his own. Wrapped tightly, I blinked beneath the kitchen's glow. That moment marked our meeting. Since then, we have remained inseparable. At times I lose awareness that he still inhabits my body—that skeletal dwelling housing my beating heart. His mother's solid character lives within me too, a foundation I carry forward. I've come to understand what was passed down to me as birthright. Through my mother's recollections, I absorbed his mother's philosophy: A pot of stew simmered constantly on her stove, available to anyone who needed it. Though she avoided church, she insisted goodness didn't require it. During the Depression era, she fed wandering transients, her back porch known as a reliable resting spot. She believed all people deserved rights regardless of skin color, and she valued courtesy above all. That woman's son—my grandfather—continues his journey alongside me even now. Something in our shared blood, some warmth, still leaps across the years separating us. Listen closely: these lungs, fashioned from his, draw breath even now. His bloodline still flows, alive, through this very hand of mine.
outputs.L3:
# Echoes of Blood and Memory

For as long as I can remember, he has been with me. My Native grandfather, with his hair as black as coal, has occupied a space in my consciousness since my earliest days of infancy—not as a distant ancestor known only through stories, but as a felt presence, woven into the very fabric of my being. I could not tell you when this awareness began, because it seems to have always existed, predating my own capacity for memory itself.

The proof of this connection is not merely spiritual or imagined; it is written into my flesh. My mother, studying my face one day, pointed to my chin and then to an old photograph, showing me how the same distinctive cleft appears in both places—a small indentation that serves as an undeniable, physical signature of lineage. In that moment, genealogy became something I could touch, a truth confirmed not through documents but through the mirror of my own reflection.

Yet my inheritance extends beyond my grandfather alone. From his mother—my great-grandmother—I carry something perhaps even more foundational: a sense of birthright, a physical framework upon which my identity has been built. She exists in my body as surely as she once existed in the world, her bones and blood having shaped the very structure I now inhabit.

What has been passed down about her, through the fragile thread of family memory, speaks not just of appearance but of character. She was known for her kindness, for a moral clarity that expressed itself in action rather than mere sentiment. She fed the poor when she had little enough herself. She extended respect to all people, regardless of the color of their skin or the god they prayed to, understanding instinctively what many struggle to learn: that human dignity knows no such boundaries. These were not abstract virtues to her, but lived practices, and they have trickled down through generations until they reached me, still carrying something of her original intention.

When I consider my grandfather now, I do not think of him as separated from me by death or decades. I feel him instead as continuous with my own existence—my breath an extension of his breath, my blood a continuation of his blood, still moving, still warm, still carrying forward whatever essential thing made him who he was. Time collapses in this understanding. He is not behind me in some fixed historical past; he is present within me, alive in the very mechanics of my living body, in every inhale and every heartbeat that keeps me here.
outputs.L4:
# Blood Memory

I never met my grandfather. He died before I could form the words to ask him about the land, about the stories, about the silence he carried in his shoulders like a second skin. And yet I know him—not through photographs alone, though I have studied the black and white image of his face until I could trace it in the dark, but through something less tangible and more insistent. I know him through my own hands.

When I look down at my fingers, I see his fingers. The particular way my knuckles bend, the breadth of my palm, the color that deepens in summer and refuses to fully fade in winter—these are not mine alone. They are borrowed, or perhaps more accurately, they are lent across time, passed hand to hand like a smooth stone worn by the exact pressure of everyone who held it before me. My cheekbones sit high the way his did in the one photograph that survived the fires and the moves and the decades of forgetting. My eyes hold the same darkness, a darkness that isn't empty but full, the way a night sky is full even when you cannot see the stars.

He was Native American, born into a world that told him his existence was an inconvenience, that his language was a threat, that his ways of understanding the earth were superstition to be educated out of him. But his mother—my great-grandmother, a woman I never knew except through the stories that trickled down like water finding its way through rock—she taught him something the world could not erase. She taught him that every person, regardless of the blood in their veins or the color of their skin, deserved to be seen. She taught him compassion not as an abstract virtue but as a daily practice, a way of moving through a hostile world without becoming hostile yourself.

He carried her teaching in him the way I now carry his cheekbones, his eyes, his hands. It became part of his marrow, and somehow, impossibly, it became part of mine. I did not learn compassion from him directly—he died before he could tell me these things in his own voice—but I find it in myself anyway, this instinct toward equality, this refusal to see hierarchy where the world insists I should. I wonder sometimes if this is simply how I was raised, the values instilled by parents who themselves absorbed them from him. But it feels deeper than that, more physical, as if the lesson is written not just in what I was taught but in what I am made of.

This is what I mean when I say blood remembers. Not literally, not in some mystical sense that defies biology, but in the way that a family becomes a river, and a river carries everything upstream of it—the silt, the minerals, the memory of every rock it has ever moved around. I am downstream of my grandfather. I am downstream of his mother, and her mother before her, back through generations I will never know the names of, back to people who watched this same land before it had the borders and names we now assign to it.

When I breathe, some part of me believes he breathes. Not as ghost, not as haunting, but as continuation. The air moves through lungs shaped by genetics he passed down, and in that movement, in that involuntary, endless rhythm of inhale and exhale, he persists. My blood moves through veins that trace the same pathways his did, carrying oxygen the same way, sustaining life the same way, and in that mechanical, biological repetition, there is something that feels sacred. My bones, too—the architecture of my body, the frame that holds me upright and lets me move through the world—these are structured according to a blueprint he once wore as his own skeleton.

Death, I have come to understand, is not the clean ending we imagine it to be. It does not erase a person so much as it disperses them, scatters them into the people who carry their genes, their habits, their half-remembered lessons about how to treat a stranger, how to see dignity in every face regardless of what the world says that face is worth. My grandfather lives, not in some other realm I cannot access, but here, now, in this body that is somehow both entirely mine and entirely inherited.

I think about this most when I catch my reflection unexpectedly—in a window, in still water, in the black screen of a phone before it lights up. For just a moment, I see not myself but him, or some blur between us, some collapsed space where past and present refuse to stay separated. In these moments I understand that lineage is not a line at all, not the straight arrow we draw on family trees, but something closer to a spiral, or a knot, where those who came before us remain knotted into the fabric of who we are, indistinguishable thread from thread.

He is in my breath. He is in my blood. He is in the very bones that will one day return to earth, just as his did, just as his mother's did before him—earth that will remember us the way we remember them, holding what we were within what we become, generation folding into generation, the dead speaking softly through the living, saying: *you are not separate from us. You never were.*
outputs.L5:
# On Walking Native, Sometimes

There's a particular kind of walking that happens when you know a place intimately—when your feet find the cracks in the sidewalk without your eyes needing to look down, when you turn corners before consciously deciding to. This is walking native: moving through a landscape as though it were an extension of your own body, unremarkable and unnoticed precisely because it has become so familiar.

But "sometimes" is the word that complicates everything.

Sometimes we walk native even in places we don't belong, adopting the rhythm of locals as a kind of costume, hoping to pass unnoticed. Sometimes we return to places we once knew intimately and find that our feet have forgotten the way, that the native walk has become foreign, halting, uncertain. The sidewalk cracks have shifted. The corners feel different now.

And sometimes, in our own hometowns, we walk like tourists—suddenly seeing the buildings we've passed a thousand times, noticing the strange angle of a streetlamp, the color of a door we never registered before. This is walking native in reverse: the estrangement that comes from too much familiarity, or perhaps not enough attention.

There's something valuable in this oscillation. To walk native all the time would mean never truly seeing where we are—our environment reduced to muscle memory, background noise. But to always walk as a stranger would be exhausting, unsustainable, a constant state of vigilance.

Perhaps the healthiest way to move through the world is exactly this: sometimes native, sometimes not. Sometimes letting the body lead because it knows the way, and sometimes forcing the eyes open, insisting on strangeness, walking as if for the first time through streets we've walked a thousand times before—if only to remember that we are, in fact, walking somewhere, and not merely passing through.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about carrying the presence of a deceased Native American grandfather within one's own body and identity.
counterfactuals.output:
**What He Left in My Hands**

Grandfather did not die.
He moved into the marrow,
took up residence
behind my sternum
where I keep the things
too heavy to name.

I did not know I carried him
until my hands began to move
the way his moved—
slow over wood,
patient with knots,
the same pause before speaking
that made people lean in
to hear what mattered.

Some nights I catch my reflection
at the wrong angle
and there is his jaw,
his particular silence,
the crease between the eyes
that meant he was listening
to something underneath the noise.

He is in the cadence
when I tell a story twice
before I let it land.
He is in the way I check the sky
before I check my phone.
He is in the ache
that has no address,
that surfaces when the geese fly south,
when someone else's grandfather
gets buried on the news
and my chest goes hollow
like a drum before the first strike.

They took so much—
language folded into silence,
land drawn into borders,
names bent to fit
paperwork that was never made
for people like us.

But they could not take
the shape of him from my shoulders,
could not take
the low hum he left
in my rib cage,
a frequency
only I can hear,
that says:
*you are not the last of anything.
You are the next of everything.*

I carry him
the way a river carries
what the mountain gave it—
not as weight,
but as direction.

I am the shore
he never got to walk.
I am the word
he swallowed
so it could be planted
somewhere safer.

I open my mouth sometimes
and it is his breath
finding new air,
his hands
finding new work,
his eyes
finding new light
to remember the old light by.

This is how the dead
stay unburied—
not in ground,
but in gait,
in gesture,
in the grandchild
who did not know
they were praying
until they realized
they were breathing
in his rhythm
all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem exploring inherited memory and ancestry, where a grandmother's moral teachings are passed down through a parent's stories.
counterfactuals.output:
# What She Left in Words

My mother speaks in borrowed voice sometimes,
and I hear another woman's cadence there—
a grandmother I never touched or knew,
alive in how my mother holds a chair
for elders, how she never wastes the bread,
the way she says *be humble* like a prayer.

*She used to tell me,* Mother starts, and then
the kitchen fills with someone from before,
a woman shaped by hunger and by war,
who learned that kindness costs you nothing more
than pride, and pride was something she could spare.

I never saw her hands. I know them still—
how they must have moved to soothe, to warn,
to shape a daughter's understanding of
what mercy meant when there was little to give.
I inherited her sternness secondhand,
her softness translated through decades worn
smooth as the counter where my mother stands
repeating what was said to her at dawn.

This is how the dead keep speaking: not
in ghostly visitations, not in dream,
but folded into small instructions—*don't
forget who raised you, don't forget to eat
before you judge another person's plate.*
The lessons come to me already creased
from other hands, already translated once
from field to city, village into state,
her language into ours, her ache
made into aphorism I repeat

to children I don't have yet, if I'm lucky,
who'll hear their grandmother's dead mother's voice
inside my voice, not knowing where it started,
only that some current moves beneath
the surface of our common blood and choice—

a woman none of us will call by name
who taught us anyway what mercy costs,
what bread means when you've known what it's like
to go without, what humility protects.

I did not know her. Still, some mornings I
catch myself softening before I speak,
some old geometry of patience learned
before I existed, handed down and down
through women who made sure the lesson turned

to instinct, turned to something in the blood
that doesn't need her name to know her love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a personal narrative about feeling a grandfather's spirit walking alongside you, blending physical inheritance (like a cleft chin) with spiritual presence.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inheritance

I have his chin, they tell me,
that stubborn cleft dividing bone
like a river choosing its course
before I ever learned to walk.

Mother says I frown the way he did—
that furrow between the brows
when the crossword got difficult
or the news turned bad again.

I never knew him.
He died three winters before I breathed,
became photographs and stories,
became the shape of my own face
staring back from bathroom mirrors.

But some evenings, walking home
when the light goes amber-thin
and shadows stretch too long
for the hour, I feel him there—

not beside me, exactly,
more like beneath my skin,
in the way I pause at corners
he apparently used to pause at,

in the way I hum some tune
nobody taught me,
that Mother says was his,
that he used to whistle
walking home from work.

I carry him in cartilage and bone,
in this cleft chin passed down
like a small inheritance of flesh,
but also in something looser—

a certain tilt of head
when I'm listening hard,
a patience with slow mornings,
a way of loving coffee black.

Grandfather, I never met you
but I meet you every day
in mirrors, in old photographs,
in the surprised recognition
on my aunt's face when I laugh.

You walk with me in ways
I can't quite name—
not haunting, nothing so dramatic,
just present, like weather,
like the blood doing what blood does,

carrying you forward
into rooms you never saw,
into a future you helped make
simply by being made yourself,

by passing down this chin,
this frown, this humming
of some old song
I never learned to learn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a reflective poem about generational connection, using imagery of bone, blood, and breath to describe how ancestors live on within us.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains

I carry them in the architecture of my hands—
the same crooked thumb my grandmother cursed
and blessed in equal measure, kneading bread
before dawn broke over fields she'd never own.

Bone remembers what the mind forgets.
This femur, this jaw, this ridge of brow
were quarried from a line of women who bent
but did not break beneath the weight of harvest,
of birth, of burying husbands and sons
in soil that swallowed their names but not their marrow.

I am a museum of small inheritances:
my father's temper living in my clenched fist,
my mother's silence folded into the corners
of my mouth when grief comes calling.

Blood is the oldest language—
it doesn't need translation, only time,
pooling in the same places it has always pooled,
rushing to the surface when shame or love
demands to be witnessed. Every vein
a river system mapping back to source,
to the first heart that beat before mine
knew to beat at all.

And breath—
this borrowed rhythm, this in and out
that began with someone else's exhale,
becomes my inhale, becomes my child's
someday, this ancient relay race of air
passed like a torch between ribcages,
each generation holding it just long enough
to prove the flame still burns.

I did not invent myself.
I am a sentence continued from a paragraph
someone started before language had my name in it.
When I stand in morning light, translucent,
I see my grandmother's shadow lengthening beneath me,
my unborn grandchild's silhouette already forming
in the space where light meets skin.

We are not separate stars.
We are the same constellation,
learning new ways to shine
the old light forward.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that begins with the speaker sensing someone following them, which turns out to be a beloved ancestor whose values and physical traits they've inherited.
counterfactuals.output:
**Footsteps**

I heard them first on the gravel path behind me—
a rhythm matching mine too closely to be wind,
too patient to be threat. I quickened.
They quickened. I turned once, found nothing
but the long shadow of the sycamore
and my own breath fogging in the cold.

For three blocks I walked faster,
counting streetlamps like a rosary,
feeling the old animal fear
climb up through my spine—
that someone unseen was learning
the shape of my walking,
matching stride for stride,
close enough to touch my collar.

At the corner I stopped, spun around,
ready to face whatever waited.

There was no one.

Only my hands, trembling—
my grandmother's hands, I realized,
the same square knuckles,
the same stubborn thumb
that could not stay still in prayer.

I looked down at my shoes,
planted the way she planted hers,
weight settled back on the heels
like a woman who has decided
not to be moved by strangers or storms.

And I understood, then, whose footsteps
had been matching mine—
not a stranger's, but hers,
sixty years gone, still teaching me
how to stand my ground,
how to give away my last coin
before I'd admit I was afraid,
how to love loudly
and forgive quietly,
how to walk into a dark street
like it already belonged to me.

She had been following
the only way the dead can follow—
inside the cage of my ribs,
behind the bridge of my nose,
in the stubborn, tender
architecture of my hands.

I stopped being afraid.
I let her catch up.
We walked the rest of the way home together,
one shadow, one gait,
her voice inside my voice
saying *good, good, keep going*—

and I did.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
